speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MESSAGES OF CONGRATULATION FROM COMMONWEALTH PARLIAMENTS
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform hon. members that messages have been received from a number of commonwealth parliaments extending congratulations and good wishes to the House of Commons and to Canada on the occasion of our centennial.
These messages have been addressed to the house by the New Zealand House of Representatives, the Senate and House of Representatives of the Australian parliament, the House of Representatives of Trinidad and Tobago, the National Assembly of Basutoland, the House of Representatives of Ceylon and the National Assembly of Kenya.
I know hon. members will want me to reply expressing our thanks to our colleagues in the commonwealth legislatures for their generous communications.

MR. GREGOIRE-REQUEST THAT RECORDS SHOW MOTION ADOPTED ON DIVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege with regard to the accuracy of the Votes and Proceedings of this house, and I do so both in my interest and in the interest of all members of this house.
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, a motion for the presentation of an Address to Her Most Excellent Majesty Elizabeth II was agreed to. That motion was passed by the House of Commons, but only on division, as I shall indicate in a few minutes. The fact that the motion was passed on division is not mentioned at all in the Votes and Proceedings of the Canadian House of Commons for its sitting of Wednesday, June 28, 1967, that is yesterday. And that is the correction I want to be made in the Votes and Proceedings.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, at the end of my remarks on this motion, as indicated in the last paragraph, I said:
But as far as this motion is concerned, Mr. Speaker, if it is carried, I ask that it be on division.
Further on, the following words appear:
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: MR. GREGOIRE-REQUEST THAT RECORDS SHOW MOTION ADOPTED ON DIVISION
speechtext:
On division.
Therefore, it is clear, and clearly stated in Hansard, Mr. Speaker.
Further, in the same text I had indicated a couple of times my objection to the motion. For instance, I said, as reported on page 2061 of Hansard, and I quote.
If it is agreed to, I would like the words "on division" mentioned-
Further on I again stated:
However, when the motion is presented and the words "on division" are mentioned, I beg Her Majesty the Queen of England to believe that I have nothing against her personally; on the contrary. I wish her a pleasant stay in Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is a quantity of precedents showing that when a motion is passed on division it must be mentioned in the Votes and Proceedings. I have some examples here taken during this second session of the 27th parliament.
On page 71 of the Votes and Proceedings of May 25, 1967, we can read the following:
On motion of Mr. Pennell, seconded by Mr. Trudeau, it was ordered, on division-that-
The words "on division" are mentioned. Why? Because we see on page 551 of Hansard of this year, and I quote:

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. GREGOIRE-REQUEST THAT RECORDS SHOW MOTION ADOPTED ON DIVISION
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

subtopic: MR. GREGOIRE-REQUEST THAT RECORDS SHOW MOTION ADOPTED ON DIVISION
speechtext:
No.

June 29, 1967
Privilege
Therefore, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) was the only one on that occasion to say "no" and the words "on division" were mentioned in the Votes and Proceedings. That is a precedent.
Therefore, knowing the hon. member for Kootenay West as I do and since his dissenting voice was registered in the Votes and Proceedings, when he was the only one to oppose the passing of a motion, I am sure that he will support my request to the effect that my opinion or my point of view should also be mentioned in yesterday's Votes and Proceedings.
I could also refer to the Votes and Proceedings of the sittting on Wednesday, June 7, and I quote:
After debate, the said report was concurred in, on divisionbecause an hon. member had mentioned "on division", as indicated in Hansard.
Another precedent can also be found in the Votes and Proceedings of Thursday, June 8, 1967, as well as in those of Friday, June 16, where the words "agreed to on division" or "passed on division" are again mentioned.
During the sitting of June 20 last, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) was the only member to oppose a motion moved by the hon. member for Riviere-du-Loup-Temiscouata (Mr. Gendron), as reported on page 1711 of Hansard, and I quote:

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. GREGOIRE-REQUEST THAT RECORDS SHOW MOTION ADOPTED ON DIVISION
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the said motion?

subtopic: MR. GREGOIRE-REQUEST THAT RECORDS SHOW MOTION ADOPTED ON DIVISION
speechtext:
On division.
Now, the Votes and Proceedings for the same day indicated that the motion was carried on division.
Mr. Speaker, since the hon. members for Winnipeg South Centre and Kootenay West had the benefit of having their dissent recorded in the Votes and Proceedings, I should like to ask for the same privilege, the same right, with regard to the dissent I recorded yesterday to the motion, namely that a correction be made to yesterday's Votes and Proceedings, so as to show that the said motion was passed on division.
There are also other precedents, Mr. Speaker. If we refer to the standing orders of the house, we find that there is no specific section in the standing orders of the House of Commons of Canada, and reference must be made to the standing orders of the house of commons in London. Now, Mr. Speaker, it can be seen that in the British parliament, the mother of parliaments, where first appeared
[Mr. Grfegoire.l
parliamentary life as we know it today, there are currently independent members from Scotland and Wales, and their rights and privileges are respected in fact, everyone makes it a point to respect them.
Well, that is a precedent that must be of considerable import for all those who, like me, have faith and believe in British parliamentary institutions.
Now, in closing, I should like to say that it was the opinion of all to vote an address yesterday. That is stated in the Votes and Proceedings, it is the opinion of all. But my own opinion, to the effect that it was passed on division has not been mentioned. To my mind, this must be corrected. Therefore, I ask you to see to it that this correction is made. The Speaker of the House of Commons, whether here or in London, is first and foremost the protector of the rights of the members and particularly of the minorities.
If there is a weak minority, a small minority in this house, Mr. Speaker, it is surely the member for Lapointe, because I am the only one who thinks in this way, and proof of this is that I was the only one to call "on division". In the circumstances, being the weakest of all minorities in this house, I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to perform your duty towards me, to protect my rights and privileges, and to insert in the Address and in the Votes and Proceedings that this motion was passed on division. If you want my name to be recorded, Mr. Speaker, I have no objection.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. GREGOIRE-REQUEST THAT RECORDS SHOW MOTION ADOPTED ON DIVISION
speechtext: The hon. member raises an interesting point of procedure and I can assure him that I will not fail to consider it. I have taken due note of his suggestions. He suggests that this dissent, the fact that he objected yesterday to the motion introduced must be recorded in the Votes and Proceedings. He is requesting that this be done also with regard to the Address. In my opinion, there is no question of recording as an appendix to a resolution passed by this house the dissent or the refusal of an hon. member, even of a minority group of hon. members. The hon. member might have a point which deserves to be considered as far as the Votes and Proceedings of the House of Commons are concerned, and again I assure him that I will be pleased to study the suggestion he has just made.

subtopic: MR. GREGOIRE-REQUEST THAT RECORDS SHOW MOTION ADOPTED ON DIVISION
speechtext:
May I take it, Mr. Speaker, that this will be reported in today's Votes and Proceedings?

subtopic: MEASURE TO REPLACE EXISTING CUSTOMS TARIFFS
MEASURE TO REPLACE EXISTING CUSTOMS TARIFFS
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-144, respecting customs tariffs.

subtopic: MEASURE TO REPLACE EXISTING CUSTOMS TARIFFS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: MEASURE TO REPLACE EXISTING CUSTOMS TARIFFS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am always apprehensive about introducing a bill which contains a very radical idea. I have learned that reform should be undertaken by very gentle measures. However, this bill introduces a new concept of export-import parity in place of the old idea of tariff control. In my usual style it would repeal all the old act and replace it with a brand new measure.
Inquiries of the Ministry
The purpose of the bill is to do away with tariffs as a punitive measure to restrain the importation of goods into Canada. Instead the bill introduces a system by which the amounts formerly paid to the government by importers by way of penalty will be directed to Canadian exporters as an incentive.
In dealing with Canada's balance of trade with other nations this bill discards the old assumptions that the sale of natural resources could validly be considered as part of a favourable balance of trade on the part of Canada, and adopts a new proposition that if Canada is to maintain a trade balance with other nations it must be done on the basis of equating dollar labour contents of goods imported with the dollar labour content of goods exported.
Motion agreed to and bill read first time.

Mr. Speaker, the other question I have for the Prime Minister has to do with the suggestion made a couple of days ago that there might be the possibility of a discussion between King Hussein and the Prime Minister particularly with reference to the position of the Arab refugees. Is it possible that such a meeting might take place? If
June 29, 1967

not, would the Prime Minister give more particulars than the generalities we have had to date concerning the extent to which Canada is prepared to accept refugees?
Second, because King Hussein is king of that portion of Jerusalem which has now been taken over by Israel administratively and municipally, will the Prime Minister say whether Canada supports the stand taken by Israel that the entire city of Jerusalem should fall under the jurisdiction of Israel, a claim which I think is reasonable under all the circumstances.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-INQUIRIES AND STATEMENTS ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext:
I think there are three questions with which I have been asked to deal. The first concerns a possible discussion with King Hussein, who is in the United States at the present time, and who I understand is leaving for his homeland tomorrow evening. It has been impossible to arrange a meeting between King Hussein, myself and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who are in Ottawa. However, our ambassador to the United Nations has seen the ambassador from Jordan in New York and will be seeing King Hussein himself tomorrow in New York to talk with him, on behalf on the government, before he returns to Jordan.
So far as the question of refugees is concerned, I can only reiterate what I have already indicated; that is, Canada is willing to play her full part in any international effort to liquidate this problem, which consists of more than one aspect. I cannot be definite with regard to the number of people we would be willing to accept into Canada as part of a United Nations scheme until discussions have proceeded much farther than they have at the present time.
So far as the situation in respect of Jerusalem is concerned, this is a matter which also, as I have said, is under consideration. Our view has been made quite clear that there should be some international control and supervision of the holy places in Jerusalem. We would certainly regret any unilateral action taken by Israel or anyone else which would make this difficult, let alone impossible.

June 29, 1967

Mr. Speaker, these estimates have been considered in some detail in committee at which time I made a lengthy statement with regard to both the customs and excise and taxation divisions of my department. Formerly there was a deputy minister and only one assistant deputy minister. I should like to congratulate all of the officers in my department for the fine work they have done. I should point out that on the taxation side the cost of collecting $100 has consistently diminished over the years, from a high of $2.06 per $100 collected in 1950 down to the present day when it costs 85 cents for all administrative and other expenses to collect $100.

Mr. Chairman, as the minister indicated, these estimates have been before the finance, trade and economic affairs committee where a number of questions were asked. It is unfortunate that we do not have the transcripts of the proceedings available to hon. members as this may bring forth some superfluous questions which have already been asked and answered in the standing committee.
I think that this could be an object lesson for the house leader in so far as his plan to rush through the estimates is concerned. If

the idea is that estimates shall continue to be sent to the committees for examination, then they must not be brought back before the house until the administrative processes have had an opportunity to put into the hands of all hon. members the transcripts of the proceedings before those committees. Otherwise we are faced here with an exercise in frustration. Even those of us who are members of the committee cannot attend all sessions which are held, and we cannot be expected to remember all of the questions asked and the answers given. So the proceedings here are either a sort of gentle waltz or the other kind of waltz, in which case we will have a repetition of what has happened today.
I trust that the Minister of National Revenue will emphasize to his colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who at the moment is otherwise occupied with other matters, that this is a fundamental point. Unless the transcripts of proceedings before committees which have examined estimates are put into the hands of members-I appreciate there is an obvious time lag because of administrative requirements-it is complete nonsense to call the estimates of a department for consideration by the committee of supply. We just waste our time.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, and without emphasizing it further, there are some questions I should like to ask the minister with regard to customs and excise and the proposed reorganization of the department in terms of decentralization. The minister indicated that there are to be six regions, 22 customs districts and 35 excise tax districts. First of all, I would appreciate knowing what these regions are and where the regional headquarters will be situated. If I hear the rumour rightly, Regina is being considered for western Canada. Without downgrading the city represented by my colleague from Regina City, I feel that administratively for customs and sales tax purposes Regina is one of our smaller centres and that in actual fact we could deal with Ottawa just as quickly as we could with Regina. As a matter of fact, I think Ottawa can be reached by mail just as quickly as Regina. Therefore I am wondering whether this move really makes sense. As I say, I do not want to downgrade Regina, but from the point of view of volume of business Regina is not one of our leading centres compared with Winnipeg, Calgary or Edmonton.
In the matter of customs districts, there again I should like to know where the headquarters of these customs districts will be located. Rumour has it that Calgary may be

chosen over Edmonton for the province of Alberta. I believe the figures will show that the volume of business in Edmonton vis-a-vis customs and sales tax is greater than in Calgary. So why choose a city of lesser population and business volume as the district headquarters? There is very definitely a much greater population in the north central part of the province than in the south central portion. So why has Calgary been picked over Edmonton? Perhaps this is a local consideration, but I am sure that the same situation will be found elsewhere. speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would be pleased to deal with the questions raised by my hon. friend. First of all, with respect to the customs and excise regional offices that are being established, the first one was established in London, Ontario. They are being established in certain locations not because of the volume of business in a particular area but rather because the place in question is a central point where contact with the rest of the area can best be made. There will be another one established in Vancouver, one for the prairie region in Regina, one in Toronto, one in Montreal with a sub-office in Quebec city, and one in Halifax for the maritimes.
With regard to the 22 district offices, I can give my friend the names if he wishes in a moment or two. Again these are locations which are close to a fairly large number of ports-importation points-and have not been chosen because of the volume of business in the particular area. The anticipated system of operation is that the ports will be in touch with the district office, and the district office with the regional office. This is why they are located in specific areas.
The officials in my department carefully studied the western provinces, about which my hon. friend was most concerned, before coming to the conclusion that the regional office should be established in Regina. I point out that this does not take anything away from any other port. We are really trying to 27053-135

Supply-National Revenue establish these offices as sub-offices of the main Ottawa office so that information is closer at hand to those in a particular area. That is the sole purpose of these offices. It does not mean that we shall take people from Edmonton, for example, because we are establishing an office in Regina. The people in the Regina regional office will be head officer personnel, capable of giving information on the spot to those involved with them.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
We entered into this operation after a test run of about one year's duration at London, Ontario. We found that the test worked successfully. We are pleased, and I believe the people in that part of Ontario are pleased, with the improved service that has come about because the regional office was established.

May I ask a supplementary question? I do not know what the attraction is in London, Ontario-perhaps it is the United States border-but can the principle that applies to the London office be applied to offices in western Canada? The whole of the northwest operates out of and through Edmonton, Alberta. I am wondering whether there is to be a difference in opportunity for contact. That was the point I was concerned about. What about the northern points? Must they report to Calgary? While the principle may have applied to London, Ontario, I feel that it need not necessarily apply elsewhere. This is not like saying that what is good for General Motors is good for the United States and what is good for London, Ontario, is good for western Canada. That is not the point when it comes to communications. With regard to Edmonton and Calgary, it is just as easy to reach either centre by flying from Winnipeg or taking a train from Winnipeg or driving. The distances from Winnipeg are practically the same. I am wondering what principle should apply with regard to the district offices. If there is any downgrading, is it not true that a senior collector, say, from Edmonton will be transferred to Vancouver and that a junior collector from a lower level will be brought to Edmonton?

speechtext:
I can indicate the present intention. We have not established those offices but I can tell the hon. member where it is intended to establish them. As I say, they have not been established yet except in Ontario. In that province they operate at Fort Erie, Hamilton, London, Niagara Falls, Sarnia and Windsor. The proposal for British Columbia is that they be established at Pacific Highway, Vancouver and Victoria. To cover north central Ontario, coming under the Toronto office, they would be at Ottawa, Sault Ste. Marie and, of course, Toronto.
Under the Halifax regional office present thinking is that district offices will be at Halifax, Saint John and St. John's. A final determination has not been made and I shall be pleased to hear representations from my hon. friend or anyone else until the final decision is made. Suggestions for the locations of district offices have come from officials in the department and are based on their studies of the clustering of ports and how those ports can be best serviced through a district office.

Mr. Chairman, with the indulgence of the committee may I ask the minister to give a detailed explantion about the

DEBATES	June 29. 1967
principle of the matter I am about to raise. For a long time it has seemed to me that different departments of government have differed in interpreting various statutes with regard to whether a man is married or single. That may sound a strange statement but I submit it is true. While some departments of government maintain that a man is married, under certain circumstances the Department of National Revenue, even though a man has a wife and dependants, says that for income tax purposes he is single. How does this differentiation come about? Income tax is the heaviest burden a man must bear. Why should the income tax authorities say that a married man who has a wife and children to support is under some circumstances single?
May I give an example to illustrate my meaning. Let us take the instance of a man born in Canada who marries a girl from the United States who is a divorcee with two children from her previous marriage. She comes to Canada with the two children and lives with her husband in Vancouver. From that marriage is born a third child. The family now consists of the natural born Canadian husband, his wife, and three children. For various psychological and other reasons the home breaks up and the wife with her three children goes back to her home in the United States. Her Canadian born husband supports her and the children by sending $200 a month. He has complete records from the bank of the money he sends her. He loses his job, goes to the Unemployment Insurance Commission, maintains that he is married, and the commission says to him: "Of course you are married; you have a wife and three dependant children. You are unemployed and therefore you will receive the married rate." The income tax authorities, on the other hand, say: "Oh, no, you may have a wife and three children but for income tax purposes you are single." How in the name of heaven a man with a wife and three children can be single is beyond me.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I went into this matter and found that according to income tax law deduction of his payments would be allowed provided a certificate were forthcoming from a family court. But in the case I have in mind officials of the family court tell me that no such certificate can be given because the wife and the three children are in the United States. In the absence of a court order, however, the Department of National Revenue rules that a Canadian with a wife and three children, to
June 29, 1967

whom he is paying a regular amount each month, is not married despite the fact that there is ample proof of his married status. According to the unemployment insurance regulations he is married, but the income tax department says he is not.
Try to imagine what it means to a man in this position when he is treated by the revenue department as a single man. Did you ever see such a stupid position taken? Yet this is precisely the attitude taken in a case with which I am very familiar. Why do I know it so well? I have referred to the case of my eldest son. He is considered by the income tax authorities not to be married. But let no one try to tell me that my son is not married and does not have a wife and three dependants in the United States.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
The answer is that the Income Tax Act does not determine whether a person is married or not; it indicates the circumstances in which a person is entitled to an exemption of $2,000 as having married status. That is what the act says.
If one is considering the position of a separated person, the act says that alimony or payments made in support of a family may be deducted when paid pursuant to a court order or a written separation agreement. This is the law as passed by parliament. It is the duty of my department not to make the law but to administer the law as this parliament in its wisdom has determined it should be.
Anyone who thinks that my department is not interpreting the law correctly has a right to appeal to the Tax Appeal Board, an independent body which sits all over the country. The appellant does not need to be represented by counsel. He can appear personally if he wishes and explain his case, and if the board decides that the department is acting improperly we are bound by its decision.

How can a person who is married and who has dependants be considered as not being married? How is it that under the unemployment insurance regulations he is considered to be married, while under income tax law he is not?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I would refer the hon. member to section 26(l)(a) of the Income Tax Act which sets out very clearly the circumstances in which a person is entitled to the $2,000 exemption in respect of married status. Incidentally, most of the information contained in that section is also given on the income tax form.

I have one or two brief observations to make concerning the estimates under discussion. The minister gave us some figures this afternoon in connection with the cost of collecting $100 of tax money and he told us that through the efforts of his department it had dropped from $2.06 to 85 cents. I give the hon. gentleman full credit for an efficiently run department. I have always felt that the Department of National Revenue was very efficiently rim. But I think he was misleading the committee when he put forward those figures because a reduction in the cost of collection is brought about automatically as a result of the increased amounts of money we are collecting. In other words, instead of ten men collecting $1,000 the same ten men are collecting $2,000. The cost of collection is bound to go down. I did not want the minister to mislead the committee on that score, though I still give him full credit for running an efficient department.
Turning to another subject, I draw attention to the fact that the hon. gentleman's department is responsible for collecting Canada Pension Plan money. This brings me to the point I wish to make. As Minister of National Revenue he should collect all moneys which go to the federal government. He should be collecting unemployment insurance money, he should be collecting the Canada Pension Plan money, as he is now doing, he should be collecting any other moneys which are raised on behalf of the federal government. If this were the case, all the money would be going to one central place from which disbursements could then be made as necessary to the other departments. The result, I submit, would be greatly increased efficiency.
As things are now, businessmen find they must deal with various officials from different departments all of whom ask for the production of records and cause considerable duplication of effort. He must deal with inspectors interested in unemployment insurance payments, inspectors auditing his books in connection with Canada Pension Plan payments, inspectors who wish to examine payrolls and other records in connection with income tax. Why not get all these people together and make these audits in one operation?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I should like to make a slight correction. The Canada Pension Plan audit is done by officials in my department. They do the income tax audit as well.

I hope that is the case, but there is still the unemployment insurance question to deal with. Let us have one audit carried out at one time and get down to a businesslike operation, which I am sure is what the minister wants.
I turn now to the money which is deducted in connection with the Canada Pension Plan. As hon. members know, overpayment of contributions by employees is taken into account and refunds are made. Employers, however, are not given any refund of overpayments they may have contributed. Many people find themselves in this category, for example, those who sit on county councils and are paid on a per diem basis. They are probably in business too, so they pay twice. I think also of people elected to city councils, of presidents of companies, and even of members of parliament who must often pay twice, here and at their place of business. Yet at the end of the year no refunds are made to employers although employees are given refunds when applicable.
The minister tells us from time to time that he and his officials have failed to devise a system whereby overpayments can be returned to employers. He says no refunds are made in the United States. But we are as smart as the people of the United States, if not smarter, and I see no reason for not coming up with a plan ahead of the United States. I refuse to accept that we are not smart enough to devise a scheme under which an employer would be credited with any overpayments made under the plan.
I feel keenly about this matter. It affects people in the construction business, in the restaurant business and particularly all those engaged in seasonal work. The fund has by now built up a balance of some $10 million or $12 million in overpayments, which is far from peanuts. It is up to the government to find a system whereby overpayments can be paid back to employers to whom they rightly belong.

Possibly the provinces of British Columbia and Saskatchewan may follow Alberta's example in remitting 75 per cent of the estate tax paid. But where this is not done in other jurisdictions something should be introduced to alleviate the hardship. It is all right to fix the estate tax assessment within the six-month period and have the return filed, but it should not be necessary to make full payment of the tax within that six months.
The people with whom the minister is dealing are honest. They are not trying to escape payment. I have never been able to see the rationality of insisting on full payment of estate tax within the six-month period. A move should be made to do away with that limited method.

Mr. Chairman, since it is just a couple of minutes before four o'clock and as there are several matters I wish to draw to the minister's attention, may I call it four o'clock?

subtopic: RAINBOW PIPE LINE CORPORATION

speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. C-105, to incorporate Rainbow Pipe Line Corporation-Mr. Orange-Mr. Batten in the chair.
On clause 1-Incorporation.
® (7:10 p.m.)

subtopic: RAINBOW PIPE LINE CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is a very interesting bill, as we said when it first came before us for consideration a year ago. Since the committee heard the evidence in respect of this measure we are doubly sure that we were right. We do not suggest there should not be a pipe line from the Rainbow Lake area to the refinery. All we are suggesting is that such a pipe line to carry these commodities should not be owned by three or four private oil companies.
This bill was referred to the transportation committee and, although I did not have the opportunity of attending its meetings, I have read the evidence which was made available only today. I am not even sure it was made available in the French language. Obviously there were questions in the minds of the members of that committee regarding the ownership of this pipe fine. I should like to refer to some of these questions to indicate the general feeling of at least some hon. members. It is interesting that the chairman of that committee decided that this bill was of great interest, because when the hon. member for Acadia asked a number of questions, pointed out that the major companies holding interests in this proposed pipe line were United States owned, and said that Ac-quitaine was French owned, the chairman said:
Let us not get into that, Mr. Horner. Order, please. This is a private member's bill, Mr. Horner, as you know. Mr. Horner, you are getting out of line now. You are free to vote against it.
The hon. member for Acadia then said that he just might do that, to which the chairman replied that this was his prerogative. At that time the question was put to a vote, and to indicate how impartial the chairman was, let me tell hon. members of the committee that the hon. member for Acadia asked whether the chairman had voted and the chairman

June 29, 1967
Private Bills
indicated that he was just casting the deciding ballot. Before this company receives federal authority to enter into the pipe line transmission field it will have to answer satisfactorily some of the questions in the minds of hon. members.
At another point in this report there is an indication that the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) asked a number of questions pertinent to this application and I think he stated the crux of the problem we have in mind. That hon. member asked whether this company was being established as a common carrier for the transmission of oil from the Rainbow field. He also asked the officials of the company to explain, if that was not the case, the purpose of setting up this company. Any hon. member who reads this committee report will find some very interesting information.
It appears from the evidence that three companies got together to develop this company. Someone also pointed out that there already is another provincially chartered company of the same name. The three companies involved are Imperial Oil which owns 331 per cent, Mobil Oil which owns 331 per cent, and Acquitaine which owns 30 per cent. The report then indicates that Banff Oil owns 3J per cent. It was then asked whether Acquitaine had a controlling interest in Banff Oil and Mr. Barroll replied:
My knowledge, sir, of the stock ownership of Banff Oil is such that I could not answer authoritatively.
This would indicate to me that probably only the three companies, rather than four, have the controlling interest in this proposed company. Surely the Minister of Finance should be interested in this fact and the statement made by the officials that the company is not primarily concerned with the transmission of oil but in the writing off of development costs against income tax. As stated by Mr. Barroll, the company is more interested in the possibility of expanding its revenue by increasing the volume of production than in increasing the price in the market place.
If one refers to page 6 of the committee report one will see that Mr. Bredin indicated that one of the reasons for the establishment of this company is so it can write off the costs of drilling and development against income with the ultimate objective of reducing the profits of the company and thereby reducing the tariffs. Mr. Bredin then said:
We propose to operate this with a minimum of profit, and should there be some small profit it can be written off by doing drilling or exploration work and thus there will be no tax payable. That

being so, you can ultimately lower your tariffs and the benefit of this will accrue to the producer. If you use your money to pay income tax you cannot lower your tariffs to the same extent as you can otherwise.
The hon. member for Edmonton West has been here for some time and he has been interested in the activities of the public accounts committee. I have read some of his remarks as reported in this committee report which would indicate that he was surprised about the statement that if the company operated at a minimum of profit it could use the profits for drilling and exploration work and if it did not have to pay income tax it could reduce the costs to the producer. The hon. member for Edmonton West then said:
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
I was interested in the logic that Mr. Bredin was using because frankly I find it the reverse of mine. If there are profits in a pipe line company against which it can charge development and exploration expenses it is to the benefit of the producer to be able to charge off those profits. Those profits of the pipe line are, of course, derived from carrying the producer's own crude as well as that of those on the market who come in under the common carrier. Therefore the profits are provided by your producing competitors as well as by yourself.
Therefore, to say that you are going to have as low a rate as possible for your common carrier business for your competitors in the producing field is not quite in accord with the facts.
It is not only not in accordance with the facts but it certainly is not the free enterprise system. I would say that the officials of these two companies must be very poor businessmen to allow a third company to obtain an advantage. It is not too difficult to see which company will have the advantage. I think I am safe in saying it will be Imperial Oil. I assume that Imperial Oil owns Mobil Oil, which may or may not be the case. I have had some experience with the manipulations and machinations of Interprovincial Pipe Line Company, which was considered by parliament some time ago. This company is under the control of Imperial Oil in various ways, although not in respect of stock control. I found they were not in a position to lower the price of transportation of their oil product through the pipe line because, if they did, not only would Imperial Oil gain an advantage but so would their competition. Therefore they decided it was much better to adhere to the price allowed by the National Energy Board and at the same time make profits out of their holdings in the pipe line.
I agree entirely-and it is very seldom that we do-with the hon. member for Edmonton
June 29, 1967

West that the statements made by the representatives of this company were not only not correct but were probably dishonest, unless you allow for inability or incompetence on the part of the representatives of the company. Nor can I see in the other evidence presented by the representatives of the company any information that would lead anyone to reach the conclusion that because they had a method of writing off drilling expenses against income tax they would be able to pay more money to the producers if the company was acting as a common carrier in addition to carrying its own oil.
This is a very important pipe line. In this area Canada has made several very bad mistakes. At one time we had a pipe line from Norman Wells through the Quesnel area to the coast. It was installed during the war and was a very small line, it is true. It was sold for probably less than the scrap price of the pipe. Therefore it will be seen that over the years there has been some manipulation in this area. I think it is also safe to say that in this area there has been a great deal of exploration and development of the potential.
Hon. members from Alberta seem to think that oil is a commodity that we should dispose of on the international market as quickly as possible. I was very surprised to learn that the reserves, according to the official of this company, are sufficient for only 33 years at the current rate of production. We talk about conservation in other fields but the people reaping the benefits of the development that takes place in this area are acting in a very uncontrolled manner. Our children will find that their parents have wasted a great deal of money in respect of the natural resources in the area.
For this reason I urge the sponsor of this bill and those interested in the development of the area to make sure that the granting of this licence is not in effect a licence that will allow a monopoly to operate. I think everyone will agree that to put in two or three competitive pipe lines for long distance transmission is probably not in the interest of the oil companies nor the producers and neither is it in the national interest. There must be some other interest behind the seeking of a monopoly situation. Before we grant a licence to operate this kind of monopoly I believe we should see that this common carrier does the job it should do for the many oil producers in the area.
The committee dealt with many aspects of the bill. Most of the clauses are concerned
Private Bills
with whether stocks should be split or transferred, whether the common stock should be changed to preferred stock, whether the preferred stock should be changed to common stock, and so on. We all know that a great many things can be done with stock. This raises an old problem with which we have dealt on many occasions. The question we should ask ourselves is, what does the company really want to do in this regard? They ask for the power to do a great many things. In the bill the company asks for the right to "purchase, lease or otherwise acquire and hold, develop, operate, maintain, control, lease, mortgage hypothecate create liens or other security upon, sell, convey or otherwise dispose of and turn to account any and all interprovincial, extra-provincial and/or international pipe lines and all appurtenances relative thereto for the gathering, processing, refining treating, transmitting, transporting, storing and delivering of any substances capable of being transmitted or transported by pipe line including, without limiting the generality of the foregoing," and so on. I do not understand how in thunder the company's powers can be limited if this bill is passed. The company seems to have covered about everything. Clause 6 also provides as follows:
[DOT]-transporting, storing and delivering of any substances capable of being transmitted or transported by pipe line including, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, any natural and artificial gas and oil and hydrocarbons and related substances or any of them and any products or by-products thereof and all works relative thereto for use in connection with the said pipe lines; and buy or otherwise acquire, process, refine, treat, transmit, transport and sell or otherwise dispose of-
What the company will be able to do goes on ad nauseam. They can buy houses, sell property, go into the field of housing development, make loans, and so on. This company is almost in the category of a financial institution. Very little is said about what the pipe line itself will do. I know that the financial aspects of the company are very important, but it seems to me the geographical aspects are also very important. I would have thought more questions would have been asked about the geographical aspects of the company. It seems to me that before the bill is passed we have to decide what we shall allow the company to do. The committee appears to have given more consideration to what they thought the company would do than to what is was really going to do and how it would operate in this area.
Private Bills

June 29, 1967
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
The Income Tax Act amendments that were made by the house in 1962 were originally intended to provide a better opportunity for oil exploration. The parliamentary agent goes on to say:
Prior to 1962, companies which were in the business of exploring for oil could deduct a certain amount of their exploration expenses from their revenues for the purpose of computing income tax. Some time before 1962 all these sections were amended to provide that mining companies, for example, could go into oil exploration, and vice versa. The whole scheme of the act was to provide more money for this kind of exploration.
This has been true for a long time not only with regard to the actual operation of companies but in the financial arrangements which the companies concerned made.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must advise the hon. member that the time allotted to him has expired.

Mr. Chairman, I attended the meeting of the transport committee when it was considering this bill. Although I am not a member of that committee, I felt there were certain aspects of the incorporation of this company which had to be drawn to the attention of the members of the committee. Personally I feel it is quite right to allow development and exploration companies to avail themselves of the opportunities offered them under the law and I am quite sure that everyone will agree that the 1962 amendment was put forward as an incentive for oil exploration and development. After all, not only the question of finding the oil is involved but also the matter of transporting it to the market. In many instances there were opportunities for the gathering lines to act as common carriers under the control of the oil and gas conservation board of the province of Alberta and under similar bodies in the provinces of Saskatchewan and British Columbia. I think it is only fair that a producing company should have the right to amortize some of the expenses of its exploration and development programs over its whole operation. This is provided for under the act, but it has to be clear that the exploration and development have been done.
However, there is one advantage gained by a pipe line company which is also in the business of development and production in that by being able to charge its expenses for exploration and development against its profits it has an advantage over its non-owner competitors in the production field. I have no

objection to that and all I wish to point out is that this fact does exist.
I listened with interest to what the hon. member for Timiskaming had to say with regard to pipe lines and their development. However, I must say I cannot agree with everything he said because I think some of his statements are incorrect. Rainbow Pipe Line Limited operates entirely within the province of Alberta. It is being incorporated federally in the event that the group of companies, that is, Mobil Oil of Canada, Imperial Oil Limited and Banff-Acquitaine, continue their operations farther north across the Northwest Territories boundary. In view of fact that the Zama lake area is not very far from that boundary, it is possible to foresee that within a year or 18 months this company, along with others which hold leases granted to them by the government of Canada, may undertake some development work and actually bring in some producing wells.
There is no sense in the production of oil if there is no opportunity to market it, and in the Northwest Territories there are no alternative means beyond a pipe line. There are no roads or railroads, so tanker trucks cannot be used, and therefore gathering lines must be used ultimately leading to a central pipe line. This is what has happened in northwestern Alberta.
The Rainbow pipe line is presently under construction from Zama lake to Rainbow lake and, although I stand to be corrected on this, I believe it goes down to the Mitsue lakes field north and east respectively of Lesser Slave lake. Farther to the south of this area there is the Peace River pipe line which heads west. There is at present before the other place an application for another very short pipe line which will be entirely domestically owned. I believe it is to be only about 15 miles long, which makes it much more economical, and the only sensible thing to do is to build this short length of pipe line across the British Columbia boundary to join the gathering system of northeastern British Columbia and ultimately feed out through Westcoast Transmission to the Pacific coast.
Would the hon. member permit a question? I have listened with interest to his description of the area. Could he tell me whether the Rainbow oil field is situated outside the Northwest Territories?

The Rainbow oil field is situated entirely within the province of Alberta. It is in what is known as the north
June 29, 1967

Peace River country. It is not in the Northwest Territories but along the eastern slope of the Rockies. The whole oil development starts in southern Alberta near Pincher creek. It changes from gas to oil and vice versa and the indications are that this will continue all the way to the Arctic coast as exploration locates the oil pools. The companies in the consortium intend to bring the oil, if they should find it, from north of the Northwest Territories' boundary on leases which it now holds.
I have no criticism of the plans for development. However, there are two questions which I do raise. First of all, it is a 20-inch pipe line in the Zama lake-Rainbow lake area. It is a major oil pipe line and because of the rather restricted operations in the future it seems to me there is a danger it may become a monopoly pipe line. No one else can say: We may find an oil pool in some area close by and then we will build a major pipe line all the way down to the refining area near Edmonton. Therefore for economic reasons this pipe line may become the sole pipe line. I do not quarrel with that. However, my view is that the ownership of such pipe lines should be in Canadian hands. I believe that a lesson could have been learned at the time of the construction of Interprovincial Pipe Line when ordinary Canadians did not have the chance to buy shares in it. There were large blocks of financing available to that company and they took up the major holdings.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
As a result of the lesson of Interprovincial Pipe Line, there was then the experiment of the Alberta Gas Trunk Line and the formula which developed therefrom. It was not entirely perfect but I think it was a major step forward. The crown caused the Alberta Gas Trunk Pipeline to be incorporated. There were some nominal directors. The shares were placed on the public market with a maximum allocation, I think, of 25 per person. The shares were first limited to residents of the province of Alberta, and if they took their full quota, fine. Any unused portion of the quota was to be sold on the open market, but I believe the issue was oversubscribed.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, the ordinary citizen, be he railroad car man, truck driver, or what have you, was able to buy shares. As a matter of fact, the initial issue of the Alberta Gas Trunk Line was 25 shares per person at $5 a share, representing a maximum investment of $125. But within two weeks or a little more people were able to sell them for 27053-135
Private Bills
$10 or so per share. However, the small investor was able to buy, and he had the opportunity to hang on to them for further profit. Many of them did.
This is what I should like to see take place with some of our solids and other pipe lines. I should also like to see the same happen with a line such as Rainbow from one end to the other. I am sure that the companies concerned would like to get their capital out of that pipe line because they can certainly put it to better use in other ways than by investing it in a pipe line for a long time.
The operations of the line within the province of Alberta are entirely under the control of the oil and gas conservation board. The common carrier rates are fixed by the board. The production from the wells is controlled by the board upon monthly nominations by the refineries and allocations by the board.
What the prospects are for the Northwest Territories I do not know, except that the National Energy Board, to whom application must be made for the establishment of a pipe line in the Northwest Territories to connect with any pipe line in Alberta or British Columbia, will determine the method of construction, rates and so forth of any such pipe line.
If the department of northern affairs and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources have any conception of proper conservation, then I suggest they will likely follow the Alberta plan. After all, the chairman of the National Energy Board was the chairman of the oil and gas conservation board in the province of Alberta. It is in the mutual interest both of that province and the federal government to see that there is the maximum development of oil resources and reserves. Naturally these resources have to be marketed in order to make any development program economically feasible.
According to the evidence given before the transport committee the other day, our oil reserves today will last 33 years. I do not know whether the figures took into account the tar sands resources in northeastern Alberta where the first refinery is due to go on stream some time later this autumn at a cost of something like $250 million, with a 50,000 barrels a day capacity.
These reserves are far greater than those in the conventional oil field areas of Alberta and the Northwest Territories. At the present time the Alberta oil wells are producing at about 50 to 55 per cent capacity. Many of the older wells with lighter production which have been in operation for 20 years are almost at

June 29, 1967
Private Bills
the point of shutdown because they are uneconomic under the present marketing system.
Briefly, Mr. Chairman, I would like to say I have no objection to the incorporation of this company to build a pipe line. There will have to be an application made to the National Energy Board and the board can hold public hearings. It is not as if we were giving this company the right to establish a pipe line wherever it wanted, and that by the passage of this bill we were giving the company the right to build the pipe line. Not at all. There are still several steps that have to be taken both before the oil and gas conservation board of the province of Alberta and the National Energy Board of the Government of Canada.
However, Mr. Chairman, with regard to the bill itself I referred the other day to clause 6 (c) as an open hunting licence and I do not withdraw that phrase today. As I said, I feel it would be far better if this company were open to public investment. By the term "public" I mean in the same way as the Alberta Gas Trunk Pipeline, or under some similar formula where by residents of the province of Alberta and people in other parts of Canada would have the opportunity to buy shares instead of these companies being controlled by three corporations, two of whom are United States corporations, the other one being French with a tie-up with the French government.
Notwithstanding the fact that this consortium has done a good deal of development work and has a good record, it seems to me that where you have a pipe line which I think, economically speaking, will be the only major pipe line working toward the north for many years to come, Canadian citizens as such should be entitled to acquisition of the equity holdings in that line.
I hold no brief for nationalization or public ownership by a crown agency or otherwise. I think that would be the last thing we would want in the oil and gas business. But I do feel that widespread ownership by the Canadian public is highly desirable. This is the sort of move that would detract from the alleged necessity of a Canada Development Corporation. I think that ultimately a much greater number of proposals of the sort I suggest will have to come before parliament. There should surely be much greater participation from the onset in such development by Canadian investors. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that there are any number of people in all

parts of the country who would be quite happy to invest $200, $300 or $500 in a type of operation like this or in a solids pipe line or in other types of transport utilities.
As I said before, Mr. Chairman, I do not for one moment hold any brief for public ownership by the crown. On the other hand, I believe that Canadians as such should have the right to invest in the equities of their resource development industries, and this would be one way of doing so.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I see that the Minister of Transport is in his place and I would hope he would comment on something which involves such an important aspect of our transportation system. I felt that he might give us the benefit of his views on the bill that is before us but, apparently he has no intention of doing so at the present time. May I point out that if this company is incorporated it may one day, under the terms of the bill, wish to build a pipe line to Bonavista, and the Minister of Transport might show a more active interest in it then.
I was interested in some of the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton West who gave the committee the benefit of his knowledge which arises partly from the very fact that he represents an Edmonton constituency. He has had more opportunity than most of us to become familiar with the operations of the oil industry and he has taken considerable interest in some of the financial legislation, income tax and otherwise, that has come before the house from time to time.
The proceedings of the standing committee on transport and communications on Tuesday, June 20, came into our hands today and we have not had much chance to look at the evidence in detail. I have tried to follow some of the information which was given and after I have made one or two references to the evidence perhaps I might be permitted to ask the hon. member for Edmonton West whether I correctly interpret the situation to which he referred at the outset of his remarks.
I found myself somewhat puzzled by some statements made by those presenting the case for the applicants before the committee. If I understand correctly, it is the intention of this company provided the charter is granted to be in a position to operate as a common carrier with a published rate of tariffs. That being so, it will carry the oil produced by it and as well as will be required to carry the oil produced by any other oil producers in the area that wish to use this pipe line. In that
June 29. 1967

case, the reference to the question of income tax write-offs for exploration expenses becomes of considerable interest as it relates to the position of a common carrier carrying the products of the principal shareholder as well as of other companies.
On page 6 of the committee report Mr. Bredin is reported to have said:
It is not the intention to operate this pipe line as a going concern in the sense of making a profit in itself. It is to provide a vehicle to get the oil out of this area at a low cost to the producers.
That may be a laudable objective but it seems at variance with the accepted objectives of a common carrier. So far as I know our railways, privately owned and publicly owned, have never suggested that they were in the business of moving goods for the love of it. Their intention is to make a reasonable profit from their transport operations.
After an intervention by the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) Mr. Bredin said:
We propose to operate this-
I assume he is referring to the pipe line.
-with a minimum of profit, and should there be some small profit it can be written off by doing drilling or exploration work and thus there will be no tax payable. That being so, you can ultimately lower your tariffs and the benefit of this will accrue to the producer. If you use your money to pay income tax you cannot lower your tariffs to the same extent as you can otherwise.
The hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) then said:
I would like to see how that reads in the transcript. It does not seem to add up.
Having read this part of the evidence two or three times I must agree with the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.). It still does not add up. It seems strange that you can spend money on exploration and thereby lower your tariffs as an operating pipe line company to the point where you make no profit, or to that point where your profit is so reduced that you are not liable for tax, but if tax is to be paid higher tariffs must be charged. This question, incidentally, throws into relief some of the strange provisions of corporation income tax legislation in regard to tax write-offs for exploration. Perhaps in drawing this question to the attention of the house the company in question has performed a commendable service.
If one considers a pipe line operation in the sense that the hon. member for Edmonton West considers it, as an operation which is brought into being because of the economics of the situation which enable it to operate as
Geneva Agreements
a monopoly carrier, it seems strange that the oil producing company which will control the pipe line company can manipulate the profit position of the pipe line company and expend money in exploration in such a way as to avoid paying income tax.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
I should like to thank hon. members for their kind consideration.
The final act of the Kennedy round is to be signed tomorrow morning in Geneva, thus bringing these negotiations to a formal conclusion. The resulting agreements, including the schedules of tariff concessions granted by all participating countries, can now be made public. I should make clear that these tariff cuts will not come into effect until January 1, 1968, and in many instances they will be staged over the next four years.
At the conclusion of my remarks I will ask leave to table, on behalf of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and myself, detailed information on the tariff and trade agreements of interest to GATT concluded during the Kennedy round. Everything possible is being done to ensure that the Canadian business community is made aware of these results without delay. The Minister of Finance and I will now issue a joint press announcement containing details of the agreements.
Copies of this announcement, as well as of a special issue of the department's publication "Foreign Trade" are being sent to the major trade and business associations in sufficient quantities for distribution to their member firms across the country. I am writing to the ministers of trade and industry of all provincial governments inviting their co-operation

June 29. 1967
Geneva Agreements
in joining with us in organizing seminars with business groups in their regions. I am also writing to the many individual firms which have expressed interest in particular export products in these negotiations.
Mr. Speaker, as has been indicated on numerous occasions, the Kennedy round constitutes by far the most important trade pact in history, the most comprehensive in coverage and the most significant in the extent and depth of tariff reductions. Some 50 countries, representing well over 80 per cent of world trade, participated in these negotiations.
Over $45 billion of goods and hundreds of thousands of tariff items are affected by the concessions exchanged; all aspects of world trade including tariffs and certain non-tariff barriers, and agricultural as well as industrial goods were within the ambit of the negotiations. Never before have trade negotiations of this scope, magnitude and far reaching impact taken place.
It is fitting on this final day, to pay tribute once again to the statesmanship and farsightedness of the late President Kennedy.
Hear, hear.

To his initiative were due in large part the ambitious objectives which these negotiations set themselves and which have to such a high degree been attained.
It was to be expected that the Kennedy round would be exceedingly complex and difficult, involving a great deal of intensive bargaining; indeed there were occasions through the nearly four years of negotiations when the obstacles appeared to some too great to be overcome. However, despite crises and delays, and due to the perseverance and basic good will of all the countries concerned, the issues blocking agreement were resolved.
As one who attended these negotiations in Geneva on behalf of the Canadian government at various critical junctures, may I say how much is owed to the leadership and skill of the director general of the GATT, Eric Wyndham-White, in contributing to the success of the negotiations, and to our own negotiating team under the leadership of Ambassador Sidney Pierce. The Kennedy round now stands not only as a symbol of the most sweeping advance yet made in the liberalization of world trade, but also as a model and example of constructive, forwardlooking and meaningful co-operation among the countries of the world.
For Canada, the success of the Kennedy round has wide-ranging implications, opening

new broad perspectives of expanded trade and benefiting all sectors and regions of the economy. Indeed, a dramatic and sustained increase in Canadian export trade is essential if we are to deal effectively with the common issues confronting us as regards standards of living, balance of payments, jobs and the like. The concessions granted in our own tariffs to gain greater access to other markets must be regarded in the light of the very great benefits which can accrue to Canada from expanded exporting opportunities.
Many sectors of industry where Canadian tariffs are being reduced are also the sectors which stand to benefit most from export gains. In many instances, the cuts in Canadian tariffs are in areas which will help reduce the costs of production for Canadian processors and manufacturers, as well as for consumers. That, Mr. Speaker, is important.
The export benefits obtained by Canada from its agreements with major trading partners cover, including wheat, over $3 billion of our current export trade. In the United States and the E.E.C. most industrial tariffs will be reduced to levels of 10 per cent or less. As a result of the across-the-board tariff cuts made by our major trading partners, trade opportunities will become available for the first time to a very wide range of manufactured goods-many of which will be Canada's exports of tomorrow. For Canada therefore the Kennedy round could contribute to the solution of many of our basic economic problems and set in motion the process of adaptation and restructuring which could, in time, reshape the character of the economy. There are many areas where we need more values added, more up-grading of our raw materials, and this should help.
It may well be that the Kennedy round will be regarded in the future as a crucial turning point in the transformation of Canada from a resource-based economy to one of the most advanced industrial nations of the world.
I have commented on previous occasions in some detail on the significance of the new cereals agreement for Canada's wheat trade, for the western prairie provinces, and for the economy and balance of payments as a whole. The International Wheat Council is convening a special negotiating session in Rome on July 12, with a view to revising the international wheat agreement so as to incorporate the cereals commitments agreed to in the Kennedy round.
Canada welcomes the participation of all countries with a significant interest in wheat
June 29, 19S7

trade in these negotiations, and would like to see the new agreement completed and put into operation as soon as possible.
I would like to take this opportunity to express again the government's appreciation to the members of the wheat advisory committee, representing major western producer organizations, who served as advisors to the Canadian delegation throughout the cereals negotiations in Geneva. Their counsel and guidance were invaluable.
Now that the Kennedy round is concluded, it is vitally important that every sector of the Canadian economy should exploit the new export opportunities before us. The main initiative must rest with private enterprise itself. The department is being geared to provide maximum assistance to the Canadian business community in their export efforts. There will of course be areas and sectors which may feel a sense of greater exposure to competition because of tariff reductions made to gain access on a wider basis to the markets of the world for a very broad range of Canadian products. There are bound to be some local, negative reactions. But in the overall, this is a great, positive step, and it can mean a very large net gain for the Canadian economy. I am sure our dynamic Canadian enterprise will ensure that result.

secured from the United States, the E.E.C., Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Switzerland, Spain, Japan, Korea, Brazil, Yugoslavia and Israel. This list shows the present and new rates of duty as well as the most recent trade figures. This represents all the major trading items but it is not a complete list of all concessions obtained. speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this party join with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) in the tribute he paid this evening to the late President Kennedy in connection with the announcement he made tonight, and the agreement which is being signed tomorrow. I think it is fair to say, if the results of the Kennedy round measure up to the predictions made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that the late President will have no greater memorial than the attachment of his name to these agreements.
We thank the government for making the arrangements for the statement to be made tonight and for the material to be distributed to members. We also thank the government for making the consequential arrangement for the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce to be discussed tomorrow. In other words, we can postpone any further comments in respect of these agreements until we reach that stage in our proceedings.
There are just one or two comments I should like to make at this time. The minister referred, and I believe quite properly, to the advantages which can flow to a country like Canada from increased trade, from greater opportunities to get into export markets, and from the possibility that our economic base may be shifted from one which relies largely on resources to a mixed base of resources and broad industrialization. We trust that the result will be an increase in the total wealth that accrues to Canada. We wish to make the point, however, that this is useless unless it is matched by domestic policies designed to make sure that the greater wealth which accrues to this country will be shared by all of our people; jn other words, improved trade policies must be matched by improvements in legislation in the field of social security, housing, and in all the other fields which get the wealth which we produce through to the people. It is not good enough simply to have expanding sets of figures in the Department of Trade and Commerce. We must see to it that the result is the highest possible standard of living, education, health and security for all our people. These things must be the ultimate goals of the Kennedy round.

Mr. Speaker, like the hon. members who spoke
Geneva Agreements
before me, I too wish to congratulate the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) and the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) for having given us, this evening, a general idea of the agreements concluded during the Kennedy round.
But first, I must congratulate the minister for having chosen that name or, so to speak, for having christened the Kennedy round as a memorial to the greatest president, to my mind, who ever ruled over the destiny of the United States in the social field, a president who, in his work, gave the human being precedence over the financial system.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that those agreements will enable Canada, whose population is very small but whose wealth is tremendous in natural resources of all kinds, even in the field of agriculture, to have easier access to export markets.
I deeply regret that those documents did not come to us earlier-we have just received them-which would have enabled us to analyse them and to make more specific comments on these agreements. When I look at the negotiations, I wonder what that will mean for farm, fish, forest and processed wood and paper products, more particularly in my region, which is recognized as a large paper-producing area. I believe those agreements will be welcomed throughout the province of Quebec, as well as Canada, and we will be happy tomorrow to issue some more specific opinions on these agreements.

Mr. Speaker, at this point, without having the details before us, it is not really possible to comment in any specific way or to make any sweeping statement in respect of the details of the arrangements which have been worked out in the Kennedy round and about which the minister has informed us in general terms. There are, however, one or two points which I might mention. The minister spoke about the expanding export opportunities. I believe this is one of the great challenges before Canada as we move into our second century, because not only have we tremendous natural resources but we also are rapidly becoming the great manufacturing country which our position in the world gives us the opportunity to be at this time.
There are several points about which I am concerned. These relate to the remarks the minister has made. The first refers to our tremendous imbalance of trade with the

June 29. 1967
Geneva Agreements
United States. I would hope that in some way the new tariff arrangements might help meet this problem, a little more effectively than it has been met in the last several years. Likewise I would trust that the benefits from these tariff reductions might be directly related to the consumers and to the costs of those things which the consumers must buy.
I think one of the great criticisms in respect of the automotive arrangement is the simple fact that the benefits, at least in the early years of this arrangement, were not passed on directly to the consumers. These reductions in tariffs will really lose their point unless this takes place. So I would hope that these arrangements will relate to some of the problems we face.
I should like to remind the minister and the government as a whole that one of the great problems we face in respect of trade today is far beyond that of the lowering of tariffs. I refer to the problem of international settlements and international liquidity.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Unless a new arrangement can be worked out as far as credits are concerned in this whole area of trade, then all of the tariff reductions that may be worked out will really not help to solve the problem we face. I believe it has become urgently apparent to some, if not to all countries which are major traders in the world, that unless there is a new basis of international exchange, a new opportunity in the area of international settlement, and a greater financial liquidity can be provided for the nations of the world as they develop in their respective and different areas with the increase of greater trade patterns, we are going to continue to be in trouble.
Speaking on behalf of this party, I welcome the trend that is evidenced in the tariff reductions as a result of the Kennedy round. I believe that it is not only important to our position as a trading nation, it is important to the world. We talk about peace and we think of keeping the peace in terms of military force and might. One of the greatest opportunities we have in working toward peaceful opportunities and for the development of our resources in the world, both human and material, can be gained from more free trade patterns and, ultimately, unrestricted trade for the world. In this regard we welcome this major step in that direction.
