speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. The house again in committee of supply, the estimates of the Department of National Revenue, Vote No. 5.
5. General administration and district offices including recoverable expenditures on behalf of the Canada Pension Plan, $57,833,900.

Mr. Chairman, when we adjourned the debate at four o'clock I had several points in mind I wished to bring to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue. I realize that his position is not an easy one. Certainly the public tax collector is not a position one would normally consider with much relish. However, this is an extremely important responsibility because governments have no sources of revenue other than from the taxpayers' pockets, and someone must be responsible for collecting the taxes which the government imposes.
The second phase of the responsibility of the Minister of National Revenue which is not particularly enviable is that phase relating to the collecting of taxes the minister had little to do with in design. I am disturbed about some aspects which have developed in regard to tax collecting which result in infringements upon the rights and freedoms of citizens. I am thinking particularly of small businesses in respect of which the owner and his employees must collect and keep record of the tax. I have received many complaints in this regard, and have a great deal of correspondence, which I believe is very little different from that received by other members of parliament.
It seems to me that this type of businessman is being asked more and more to devote a great deal of his working time to the services the government requires of him. This is true not only of tax collecting but in the interpretation and enforcement of taxing regulations, as well as filling out innumerable tax forms which are constantly before him. The small businessman must comply with these demands on behalf of the government, and at its request.
The Department of National Revenue must constantly keep in mind that much of this work which is being done by the small businessman is really being done as a courtesy to the Department of National Revenue. It must be understood that this very often costs the small businessman a good deal, and
June 29, 1967	COMMONS
causes him a great deal of concern. It is with this fact in mind that I introduced a bill in this house, C-130, which relates to the establishment of the position of ombudsman for administration. I suggest in this bill that this appointee could very well be the Auditor General, and in this way avoid the appointment of another official, or members of another staff. I made this suggestion because someone must better look after the interests of the small businessman and other taxpayers, as well, other than just members of parliament.
To be more specific let me refer to some of the problems which have come to my attention in recent days. First of all I refer to the exemption of the tax on drugs, to become effective on September 1 of this year. I am concerned because no provision is being made to protect the druggists of this country regarding their investment in the stock which now sits on their shelves. I have received correspondence from a number of druggists and have become aware of the fact that there are many corner drug stores, as they may be described, the owners of which will be out of pocket anywhere from $3,000 to $8,000 because no provision has been made to refund the tax they have already paid on these inventory drugs, prior to the implementation of this tax removal.
I have in mind particularly a druggist in my own town. He tells me that this revision in respect of the tax exemption on drugs is likely to cost him $6,000. He operates an average size drug store, but he expects he will lose that amount of money because no provision has been made to refund the tax he has already paid on the drugs now on his shelves. The minister has already said that no one will require these druggists to make an immediate reduction in their prices, as soon as the removal of this tax comes into effect. It is very nice to talk as the minister does, but who would sensibly suggest that such a man would be able to charge the price charged before the removal of the tax, after the tax removal goes into effect? That is not possible. Certainly the minister and his officials know that the public will expect that after September 1, 1967 the cost of drugs will come down by an amount equivalent to the tax which has been removed.
I urge the department to take some action in this regard in order to protect the small businessman who is going to pay money out of his own pocket because of this tax reduction. Surely this is not fair. It seems there ought to be some consideration given by the department for these people who do so much
DEBATES	2125
Supply-National Revenue for the government in collecting taxes and keeping records. Their plight should be considered when the tax exemption takes effect. I would urge that the department take a second look at this problem and do something about relieving the very heavy burden which will face most people in the business of selling drugs when the tax exemption comes into effect.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
I should like to mention another matter in respect of the collection of sales tax from small businesses which may be classified in part, as far as their activities are concerned, as manufacturers manufacturing items totalling more than the minimum exemption per year, which I believe is $3,000. Here again a difficulty is being worked on a number of small businesses. It is really so heavy on some that it means the difference between being able to stay in business and not being able to do so. Let me be specific and quote one example. In any city or town in this country you may find a welding shop. This welding shop is not really in the business of manufacturing, but in the course of its business clients bring to it the type of work that can be classed as manufacturing. If this type of business totals through the year more than the minimum exemption, it is necessary for the owner of the shop to collect the sales tax from those with whom he does this business. This is the regulation. If the welding shops in every community across Canada were classified and inspected by the tax department no hardship would be imposed on some that did not apply to the others. The simple fact is that because the taxation offices do not have sufficient staff to go out and check on every type of business that might come under this classification or category, some are registered and are required to pay tax and others are not.
What disturbed me about the attitude of the department is this, and I hope the minister takes note of this problem. The tax department says, when you bring this matter to their attention: We do the best we can about bringing every business in this category under the inspection of the department, but we cannot be sure that we get them all. Will you please ask those shops that are complaining about having to pay the tax to tell us the names of those who are not paying it. Ask them to give us a list of those shops that are not paying the tax.
They even ask us as members of parliament to make a list of the shops that are not paying the tax. How foolish can the tax department be
June 29, 1967

Supply-National Revenue in this regard? Does this mean that a member of parliament should become a policeman for the tax department? Does it mean that a man has to make a report to the department about those with whom he competes? Certainly the clientele of these shops will not accept this. It is not the responsibility of the businessman or the member of parliament to check into these matters for the tax department. If the department does not have sufficient staff, or is otherwise unable to make the proper inspection to make sure whether firms in this minor category-I think this is how it might be described-are paying the right tax, it is up to the department to check into the matter.
It seems to me it would be only fair not to collect tax from one firm if the department is not able to ascertain all other firms which fall within this category. This problem applies to many communities across Canada. I am not putting forward a theoretical proposition; I am talking about a situation that exists. In many small cities and towns two, three, four or five people are engaged in the same line of business; one or two of them are paying tax and fall under the inspection of the department, and others are not paying tax and are not required to meet the regulation. Surely this is not fair.
This is a real problem that is presented to a number of small businessmen in this country. The situation is not satisfactory and something should be done to resolve it. Again I say that I believe it is the responsibility of the tax department to ascertain who should pay this tax. The department must look into the problem and not just condemn these people as complaining for the sake of complaining or trying to get out of paying tax. I do not believe that very many people in Canada try to get out of paying taxes that are required according to the law of the land. In fact, Mr. Chairman, I have found that the great majority of businessmen want to do what is right, but because of the complexity of the tax regulations and the unfairness of the application of some of these regulations they find themselves in a very difficult position. Also they find themselves in a position of tension because they are continually concerned as to whether they are properly carrying on the type of work that requires them to pay tax. They fear they may be in error and will be brought before the department for having made a mistake or for not having paid tax which they did not believe was their responsibility. I should like the minister to


give me an answer to this question before these estimates are passed, and I would urge the department to take a very careful look at the problem.
Another point is that under tax regulations certain types of equipment are classified as farm equipment. An increasing number of new machines used on farms legitimately come under the classification of farming equipment. This equipment has not necessarily been used in the past and the farmers are not being properly classified in respect of the equipment as far as tax exemption for agricultural machinery is concerned.
One such problem that has been brought to my attention, of which I have informed the minister-and I believe the department is aware of it-concerns a type of farm trailer that can be used behind small trucks or tractors. This equipment is used both commercially and agriculturally. Some farmers are required to pay the normal tax and others are exempt from it. In my opinion it is the responsibility of the tax department to make sure that the application of its regulations is equitable and fair to everybody, which definitely is not so in this case.
There is still another problem with regard to which I have not been able to obtain a satisfactory answer from the department. It concerns an item that is not yet manufactured in Canada and must be imported from the United States. This matter has been mentioned a number of times in debate. I refer to the motor vehicle that is used as a funeral coach, a hearse, or as a combination coach and ambulance. As these vehicles are manufactured only in the United States they come under a regulation that is specific in so far as tax exemption is concerned. The department has recently attempted to classify a similar unit made in St. Catharines as an ambulance and funeral coach. In the opinion of the department funeral coach and ambulance types imported from the United States would now come under the tax regulations that otherwise would not be applicable. Here again it seems to me the department should be more concerned about looking at the problem as it relates to the businessman involved or the user of the particular piece of equipment, rather than applying the regulation in all its apparent legality. In the case I have in mind a combination ambulance-funeral coach has been manufactured in the United States and brought into Canada as a vehicle to be used by a voluntary organization in the city of Jasper. It is required that a duty be paid on
June 29, 19S7

this vehicle both because of anti-dumping regulations, as well as the normal customs and excise tax.
[DOT] (8:50 p.ra.)
On top of that it is subject to other taxes, which I do not believe should apply to this type of vehicle, on the pretext that a minibus or a truck type of stationwagon can be modified by raising the roof to make it into this type of vehicle. Perhaps ambulances may be made by modifying other vehicles to meet the requirements of public health and safety, but the fact remains it is not really this type of vehicle. Again it seems to me that the decision of the department in the interpretation of regulations should be in favour of the user of this equipment and of the businessman who is responsible for importing this type of vehicle into the country.
I have one more point which I should like to bring before the minister tonight. It applies to the registration of charitable organizations to which gifts would be exempted under the income tax regulations. I think there has been a great deal of trouble with regard to this matter. I do not think anyone can be blamed for this because the legislation was only passed shortly before Christmas and the announcement that it would be implemented as of January 1 came much too soon for the necessary preparations to have been made in order to process the thousands of organizations in the country which come under the legitimate classification of charitable organizations.
I wish to commend the minister for having speeded up the processing of the larger organizations that I have brought to his attention. I believe that most of the larger organizations in the country have already been registered. However, we are six months along in the new year, and there are still hundreds of organizations, many of which have applied as early as in January, which have not yet been registered and have not had a number assigned to them which they must indicate on receipts given to those who make donations to these organizations. It seems to me that here again undue hardship was worked on the person who is not trying to evade taxes but is trying to follow the regulations and obey the tax laws of the country. It would have been far better if the implementation of this tax could have waited until the department was

Supply-National Revenue ready to process the thousands of applications which it knew would inevitably come before it. I would only hope that at this late date the department will make every effort to deal with these applications so that the receipts that are being held up for lack of a registration number will be soon available to the organizations which are legitimately classified as tax exempt charitable organizations.
There are other points that I could bring to the attention of the minister. However, the four or five points which I mentioned represent urgent problems to many Canadians. I trust the minister will give an answer to as many of them as he can while we are discussing the estimates tonight and that action will be taken to clarify them as quickly as possible.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
First of all I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Red Deer on the interesting points he raised with respect to the administration of the Income Tax Act. I should like to say to him that in the determination of tax policy there is very close co-operation between the Department of National Revenue and the Department of Finance. I would not say the Department of National Revenue ever administers a policy which it has not had the opportunity of considering previously.
The hon. member mentioned the cost of collection by small businessmen. The idea that small businessmen having to collect taxes for the government of Canada-a very interesting proposition-should receive some recompense for doing so. This matter had been considered by this and previous governments but the conclusion has been reached that to recompense the small businessman would entail an increase in taxes in order to raise the funds to pay them.

Mr. Chairman, may I clarify a point? I did not suggest the government should recompense these businessmen. The point I was trying to make is that the government should facilitate the work they are doing. I understand that paying them for doing this work is out of the question. I would only ask that consideration be given to assisting them in facing the problems which they have as a result of having to do this work.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I should like to say that the officials of the taxation division of my department try to co-operate with small businessmen as much as possible in order to simplify their task, which is a difficult one. The hon. member for Wellington South put forward an
June 29, 1967

Supply-National Revenue idea this afternoon which has been in my mind for a long time, namely that the collection of all the revenues of the federal government should be handled by one department. However there are some very difficult questions involved with regard, for example, to unemployment insurance which is handled by a separate commission. I would simply like to assure hon. members that this matter has been receiving constant consideration by the government and although legislative steps are involved we will continue to consider the matter of facilitating the work of the small businessmen on behalf of the government.
The hon. member for Red Deer mentioned the matter of the ombudsman. It is my opinion that so far as taxation in Canada is concerned we have in effect a group of ombudsmen in the income tax appeal board, a body of men quite separate from the Department of National Revenue, which travels about the country hearing taxpayers' complaints with regard to individual taxation matters. They have been most successful in their work, and I think all of us should congratulate them on the manner in which they have carried out this task over the years. This board does the job of dealing with the taxpayers very satisfactorily. As I mentioned this afternoon, I hope that in order to clear up the backlog of their work we might expand their number so that taxpayers may be given a better chance to appeal to these quasi ombudsmen.
The hon. member for Red Deer also mentioned the matter of drugs and the problem of some people who will be left as of August 31 of this year with the sales tax on drugs which are on their shelves. Basically this is a matter for the Department of Finance. It is the job of my department to administer the law as approved by parliament, and not to make the law. However, a good deal of consideration has been given to this matter, and I believe the Minister of Finance would support me on this. One of the reasons for which the tax was not reduced immediately but was delayed for several months was to give people an opportunity to review their inventory and protect themselves as much as possible. Of course it is not possible to protect oneself completely, but the other alternative would have been to reduce the tax immediately and this would have raised a far greater problem than the one raised by my hon. friend. As things stand at present pharmacists have an opportunity to adjust their inventories in order to minimize their losses.

May I ask the minister a question? He said the only other alternative

would have been to impose the tax immediately. Why not trust the druggists of this country to submit reports which would give them an exemption on the inventory of drugs on their shelves as of August 31 in order that they may relieve themselves of this very serious problem? Does the minister mean they would have to sell everything they had on their shelves, and then through some miracle replenish their shelves again on September 1? There is no logic in his argument.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
When a federal sales tax is charged, a federal law is passed and the tax becomes effective on the same day. The reason generally that this is done is that efforts are often made to minimize the effect of sales tax. The reason that the Minister of Finance -I am not trying to justify his policies; he is quite capable of doing this himself-decided upon the four month period was in order to remove any problem for the people involved.
The hon. member for Red Deer also mentioned people who pay sales tax on their production while others are exempted from that sales tax because their production amounts to less than $3,000 a year. This has been a constant problem to the customs and excise side of my department, whose estimates we passed earlier. Indeed, we have tried to seek ways of easing the problem involved.
However, arguments are made on both sides. It is argued on the one side that the $3,000 exemption is insufficient, that people should be allowed to produce goods worth $4,000 or $5,000; on the other side it is argued: "I have just exceeded $4,000 production and have to pay 12 per cent sales tax, whereas a fellow I know down the street who is moonlighting and producing just $3,000 worth of goods a year does not pay the sales tax".
Probably the simple solution, Mr. Chairman, would be to impose sales tax on all production regardless of value. The reason this is not done and that there is this exemption is an administrative one; we would have to try to deal with everyone working in production part time and who might be subject to the imposition of sales tax.
My hon. friend also raised a question about farm equipment. I think some of the problems he raised will be eased as a result of the decision of the Minister of Finance and the government to remove the sales tax on production machinery. One of the big problems that we encountered when sales tax was imposed on production machinery was due to
June 29, 1967

this. In the past people in the farming industry had considered purchasing certain production machinery, which was sales tax free. Then all of a sudden sales tax on this machinery was imposed and these people wanted this machinery moved from the category of production machinery into the category of farm machinery. I think this particular problem will be eased a little by the decision of the Minister of Finance and the government to remove sales tax on production machinery as such.
The hon. member also mentioned sales tax on funeral coaches. One of the difficulties in this regard is that not only is there a sales tax and customs duty on used cars imported into Canada, but except in special cases the importation of used cars into Canada is prohibited. Over the years I think this prohibition has been justified. In view of the vast United States market and the differential in car prices in Canada and the United States, succeeding governments have decided to protect Canadians against a flood of used cars from the United States.
I should like to inform the hon. member that some of the few exceptions which have been made to this rule against importing automobiles from the United States-and these exceptions are made pursuant to section 22 of the Financial Administration Act-were in respect of funeral coaches. The government has always taken the position that this prohibition of importation was for a specific reason, and that before allowing any less restricted importation of used funeral coaches from the United States the government must canvass the industry in Canada to see whether there was any objection.
This canvass was made, and some of the few cases where we did ease up on the importation of second-hand vehicles into Canada related to funeral coaches which were bought by people with relatively small means in this business, who imported these vehicles from the United States because they could not afford to buy new vehicles. Generally, Mr. Chairman, we have looked reasonably sympathetically toward these people in this regard.
The other point raised by the hon. member for Red Deer concerned registration of charitable organizations. I think that the staff of my department is to be congratulated on the tremendous progress that has been made-I am speaking here of my officials-in the registration of charitable organizations in Canada. When the legislation was passed last fall-legislation which I think was good, and necessary-my department was faced with
Supply-National Revenue registering some 40,000 charitable organizations in Canada. We had to decide how to handle these organizations, whether we would hire new staff to handle them, or have close consultation with the charitable organizations themselves and try to move them through in as orderly a manner as possible.
We decided to adopt the latter course, and I think this has generally worked out very well. My hon. friend indicates that there are still hundreds not registered, but in cases where non-registration of a charitable organization is causing difficulty, if the organization will get in touch with my department they will be given special treatment. However, we followed the general policy of determining in connection with these charitable organizations when they collected most of their funds. We dealt first with those who collected their funds in the early part of the year and sent their registrations out to them, and we will deal with the others when we have more time.
In cases where changes have been made and funds were collected at a different time, or where special problems were involved, when hon. members such as the hon. member for Red Deer got in touch with my department I think they would have to agree that they received reasonable and fair treatment from the department in dealing with these problems.
In conclusion I would say that I think the people in the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue who have dealt with this matter have done a tremendous job to date, and I think they are to be congratulated.

Mr. Chairman, might I make one or two comments; I think there has been a misunderstanding on one or two points I made. I was not criticizing the department in the latter instance at all. In fact, I said I found them very co-operative whenever I brought to their attention the problem of an organization which had not had its registration approved. I was drawing to the attention of the minister that many of these organizations are presented with a real problem and perhaps were not aware that they could ask for special consideration. I put forward only the cases of those that I felt really deserved special consideration in view

Supply-National Revenue of the volume of receipts that they issued. While the department may well be deserving of commendation, we have now reached the point where the situation must be cleared up very quickly.
With regard to funeral coaches, I was not talking of used coaches at all but of new coaches and some of the problems which are arising over the calculation of duty and tax. According to the regulations-I am not disputing this-if these vehicles are made in Canada-at least, vehicles of similar type, the imported vehicles would be subject to certain regulations which would not be the case if they were not made in Canada. It is understandable that the volume of demand for funeral coaches, and particularly for proper funeral coach and ambulance combinations, is such in Canada that it will be a long time before we can manufacture them here. Perhaps I did not make myself clear when I was speaking about sales tax. I was not particularly concerned about the small manufacturer, who is probably $100 over the minimum or $100 under it. I was referring to the apparent inability of the department-and this is probably owing to a lack of staff which makes impossible adequate supervision-to bring under inspection every business that is eligible to pay this tax. be paid to them, in order to alleviate the problem which affects this area.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to raise, in short order, three problems that are important. The first has to do with deductions in personal income tax. The situation in Ontario has become chaotic. Some, who receive insufficient income in one year to pay income tax, under certain circumstances receive enough revenue to pay income tax the following year, and a confused situation has arisen. The provincial department dealing with social welfare has not been able to cope with the problem that has arisen.
Another matter I wish to raise is that of simplifying the means test as it relates to the income tax form. Not all married couples live together. A man of 70 or 75 may be separated from his wife, and similarly a woman of 70 or 75 may be separated from her husband. They may have been separated for a long time. How is a spouse to know how much the other earned in any year, if that spouse cannot find the other? The department wishes to know what the combined income of the couple was. Of course, there is a form that may be filled out to show that a couple is separated and that one spouse has not supported the other; but getting involved with such a form is a complicated business and I think a simpler way of providing the required information should be found.
Perhaps on the application form a section for separated persons should be included. A number of people have asked me to get in touch with a husband or a wife, so that one could find out how much the other earned.
June 29, 1967	COMMONS
Often the information has not been forthcoming. Remedying this situation would be useful.
Consideration should be given to exempting non-profit organizations from the building tax. Specifically, I am thinking of a legion which decided to build family unit homes for some senior citizens. They had to pay the building tax. Surprisingly enough, the tax made a difference of $7 or $8 in rent. I should not think that there are too many non-profit organizations that would be affected by the removal of the tax; and I do not think tax collections would go down appreciably.
Every member of parliament, I believe, wishes for a simple income tax application form. The simpler the forms, it seems, the less even the Philadelphia lawyers can figure them out. It seems that the man in charge of the computer expects only those in the $30,000 and $40,000 bracket to be able to answer the form. Personally, I have advised people who have got in touch with me and who make that kind of money to fill out the form as best they can, send it to the department, and let the department figure out if there is anything wrong. There must be a better way of compiling tax forms and schedules.
Frankly I do not know how they calculate some taxes. I studied trigonometry, algebra and geometry, but I do not know the mathematics involved. It seems that the simpler the form is said to be, the more complicated in fact it is. The minister said that this year we should have the simplest form we have ever had. Well, even the accountants are not sure of what should be done. I should like to see the minister putting two or three of his best men to work on this problem, so that when we get our income tax forms next spring we will find forms that are simpler for us to fill out, rather than simpler from the point of view of the department.

How simple?

The only way to make it simpler is to have simpler tax laws. I know the minister is sympathetic in his attitude toward small businessmen-and here I do not have in mind the department's definition. I am not speaking of businesses handling $500,000 a year; I am speaking of small businesses handling $50,000 a year.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: As hon. members will understand, this involves a matter of tax policy which has nothing to do with administrative decisions made by my department. I have a great deal of sympathy with the plea made by the hon. member. The situation he describes does not involve liability for income tax alone; it also concerns unemployment insurance. A small businessman may not deduct the expenses of a wife, though he may deduct salaries paid to his children. And he may not insure members of his family for purposes of unemployment insurance. If his business were incorporated, he could do this, and one solution might be to file a joint return. The ideas suggested in the Carter report, on which the government has made no decision, would probably clear up this kind of problem, though they might create many others.

First, I should like to thank the minister for the personal attention he has given to any matter I have brought to his notice. This is good public relations. A number of people have written to me saying how much they appreciated having the questions they brought to my attention answered in detail by the minister or by some of his senior officials. One lady told me that she had never met anyone who could pick Canadian pockets so congenially and with such a winning smile.
I appreciate the co-operation I have had from members of the staff of the department and also from members of the staff of the district office with whom I have discussed questions in respect of my own constituency-transportation, the best way to go here and there, and so on.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer with respect to charitable organizations. I have brought this matter before the house on a number of occasions throughout the years, because I have never been satisfied that all the organizations which are registered as charitable organizations really are charitable organizations. Could the minister tell us briefly the result of the study which was made of this situation? Would it be possible for hon. members to be given the names of the organizations which are now registered as charitable organizations, together with an indication of the formula used by the department to determine their eligibility under the terms of the act?


The other thing I wanted to say was this. Although greatly increased amounts are collected in taxation every year, the efficiency of the department is increasing as a result of the introduction of various types of unusual machines. I have very little knowlege of how they work, but I have been through the building, have seen these machines in operation, and have seen the results.
It is fair to say that persons who work in a department such as the Department of National Revenue are doing something which has no drama attached to it-their work is related to figures and facts and to the interpretation of an exact law. I think the officials and the staff who work in the department are deserving of a great deal more credit than the people of Canada give them at the present time. It would make for good public relations if the Department of National Revenue would put out some booklet or pamphlet which could be sent to taxpayers when they receive their tax forms or correspondence from the department, a booklet which would indicate the vast increase which has taken place in the work done over the years and the efficiency of the staff in general in dealing with it. Some of the problems related to the administration of the department could also be drawn to the attention of the public in this way.
I offer this as a suggestion. Two or three people have spoken to me along these lines, feeling that such a move would assist the operations of the department, improve public relations and bring the administration closer to people who are more inclined to be irritated by its activities than pleased by its efficient operation of the law.

Mr. Chairman, it is difficult for me to look at the minister and not realize that he is also President of the Treasury Board. I realize, however, that on these estimates I cannot discuss a burning issue until he dons his other hat. For this reason I shall raise just one matter that comes under his responsibility as Minister of National Revenue. It is a matter we have raised before. 1 still hope it will be sorted out in a way that will cause less hurt to the people affected.
I am referring to the fact that quite a number of older people who have adjusted to a pattern of income tax payments discover that the addition of the old age security pension, or of some other pension payment, puts them into a category in which, if their tax is not paid quarterly, interest is added to it at the end of the year. The cases that have been drawn to my attention, and they have been many, all involve small amounts of money, $4, $5, $6, $7, or $8 as interest. I do not need to tell the minister how plaintive some of these letters are because I am sure he gets even more of them than I do.
I realize that the minister and the department argue that it is a kindness to people to urge them to pay their income tax quarterly rather than annually, and also that since most people have to make tax payments monthly, or even more often, through deductions at source, fairness demands that all people be treated the same way. But in actual fact what happens is that some of these people go along for two or three years without being required to do this. They make their income tax payments at the end of the year and are notified that the payments are satisfactory. Then all of a sudden comes a year when they get a bill for $4, $5, $6, $7, or $8 interest.
I am not trying to lay down the law to the minister. All I am suggesting is that the problem be looked at with sympathy for the position of these people. One suggestion I do make is that at least people be warned that this can happen. I hope the minister will not tell me that this is a matter of income tax policy. But even if it is, he could discuss it with the Minister of Finance.

I realize that old age security is taxable. At the moment I am not arguing about that. But this is the element which requires many older people to pay income tax quarterly, or to pay interest after believing they have computed the right amount of tax that they owe. As a matter of fact in all the cases that have been drawn to my attention, with the exception of the interest the taxpayers had computed their tax payments accurately. Older people have many other things to cope with, such as the rising cost of living, and it is a cruel blow when they have to pay this amount in interest. Maybe older people who are already in a different category because of the $500 extra exemption they receive over age 70, might be given a different status with respect to this matter.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would simply like to say that this problem was a very difficult one when I first became Minister of National Revenue, but it has become somewhat of a lesser problem because of some steps we have taken. One of the things we have done is that when people are sent their first old age security cheques they are also forwarded a notice telling them to look to see whether they now become subject to payment of income tax in instalments.
As my hon. friend indicated, this often is the case because these people have small incomes. They get $900 a year extra and so become taxable and subject to quarterly instalments. I am not speaking on behalf of the government on this point because I am not authorized to do so, but I would be very pleased personally if this parliament said that the Minister of National Revenue was not responsible for collecting instalment interest under $5 in amount that may be due by any individual taxpayer. This would clear up a lot of these problems, and the amount of revenue involved would not be great. However I should indicate to my hon. friend that under the existing law it is the duty of the minister and of the officials in his department to apply the law as it exists, so that if somebody owes $1.50 we have to send him a bill for it. I think it is possible to do something in this regard. Indeed we have already done something, through co-operation with the Department of National Health and Welfare, by sending out these notices with the first old age security cheques.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllrailh (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as hon. members know, the estimates of the department have been reviewed by the standing committee on housing, urban development and public works. This is the first time the estimates of the Department of Public Works were placed before an estimates committee, and I believe from my own observation that it was a useful procedure for all who participated. I also believe it will be a useful technique in the years ahead, in providing some of the detail that is desirable and necessary in order to have a critical examination of the estimates.

In addition to the opportunity to discuss the estimates in the standing committee an undertaking was given by me that when additional information becomes available later in the year on one of the main items an opportunity would be provided for the committee to get that information and deal with it, either by referring the annual report to the committee, or some other procedure of that nature. That is also a new departure and will provide an opportunity for dealing with a subject when the information is not available on the first occasion.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
The details of the estimates were prepared almost a year ago and since that time we have implemented a major reorganization of the department. The functional branches as described in the blue book, therefore, no longer exist. They have been replaced by an organization based upon the sequence of operations which applies to each project and upon a decentralization of authority to six regional offices. The sequence of operations is reflected in the headquarters directorates which are program planning, design and operations. When these three necessary functions have been completed for each project, the regional offices then assume the responsibility for constructing the work and for its subsequent operation and maintenance. A fourth new branch in headquarters is program evaluation which is important in view of the substantially increased delegation of responsibility and authority to the decentralized unit.
As I have mentioned, the duties of the administration in the blue book do not correspond with the new organization, and therefore the allocation of personnel as shown in the blue book does not correspond with the new organization. In taking together all the votes for which personnel establishments are required, we anticipate that we will be able to implement the new organization with no increase in the number of positions beyond what these positions were prior to the reorganization. In future years, our personnel establishment will, of course, have to be regulated by the work load; however, we expect to be able to handle greater work loads under the new organization without an increase in personnel.
The total increase in the estimates over last year is $15.7 million. Most of this increase is attributable to the cost of providing accommodation for other government departments. With reference to accommodation for the departments, we are working within a long
June 29, 1967

term plan which will enable us to meet the requirements of the departments by constructing new buildings and at the same time maintaining a reasonable balance with accommodation leased from private owners. There is a backlog in this activity, and the increase in our building construction appropriation reflects our efforts to catch up.
The expenditure on harbour and river engineering services in the present fiscal year will be about the same as in previous years. There are several large harbour projects under this heading such as those at Long Harbour, Newfoundland; Belledune Point, New Brunswick; and Gros Cacouna and Matane, Quebec, which are of great importance in connection with local industrial development and consequent transportation requirements. We will also, of course, be constructing a large number of small projects which are not listed individually in the details of the estimates since the requirement is that only items in an amount of over $50,000 are listed.
I could extend my remarks, but I think it probably is the wish of members of the committee that I do not do so at this stage. I shall be pleased to give all the information I can in answer to the questions which are asked. I shall be very glad to hear the views of hon. members on this subject.

time the officials said there were approximately 90 employed. With the new procedure and responsibility given to the Department of Public Works I am sure there will be an elimination of the duplication or multiplication of the work of architects, draftsmen, engineers, either mechanical or electrical, researchers, specification writers and the staff of the procurement branches of different departments.
As a result of the adoption of this policy there will be created certain agencies specialized in certain fields of activity. Surely this can only lead to savings, better administration and solutions to the problems which face so many Canadians, and I refer to the taxpayers. When the government tends to economize and continuously searches for ways and means to save the taxpayers money on behalf of the Canadian people, it is doing a good job.
How many branches of departments of government have their own architects, engineers and draftsmen? The duplication of service in this regard could be eliminated if these efforts were centralized in the Department of Public Works. There are very many services which are of a specialized nature. I am thinking particularly of services performed for the Department of National Defence. If centralization could be brought about, all the departments of government would require only a small staff with a very few consultants who could keep in touch with the officers of the Department of Public Works, who would advise them as to their requirements in respect of buildings and other things. I am sure these officers of the Department of Public Works could do this job as efficiently, with a greater savings of the taxpayers' money.
Some of the recommendations of the Glassco commission in respect of the Department of Public Works were very interesting. The first I should like to mention related to the processing and control of mail. The report suggested that statistics now reveal that the cost of processing mail is $79 for 1,000 pieces in the Department of Veterans Affairs, and $472 for 1,000 pieces of mail in the Department of Public Works. The statistics also revealed that the cost of processing outgoing mail in the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Citizenship and Immigration was approximately $2.40 and $1.70 for 1,000 pieces respectively. The statistics showed that this cost in respect of the Department of Public Works was $16.50. This amount is the result of some expensive practices. I am sure this information has been considered, but we would be

very interested to find out just how the situation has been improved.
In respect of the Department of Public Works acting as a purchasing agent for all departments of government, I believe it could specialize in the fields of construction and maintenance. In my opinion it is sensible that the purchasing for all government buildings, owned, leased or operated by the government, could be done by the same department. In looking at the same report I note there is an expression regarding the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. In the view of the commissioners the scope of the corporation's engineering activities should be limited to technical areas directly related to broadcasting.
I believe these recommendations reinforce the argument that I have been trying to advance, that one department should have the technical and professional men needed to carry out these requirements for all departments, including those associated with the acquisition of land for all departments. I am sure if the Department of Public Works had the authority and responsibility of acquiring land it could specialize in this field and act in such a way as to protect the public from unnecessary expenditures. The question of rentals and other facilities is again a specialist field. I am sure that if the department took on the responsibility for all leasing we would receive much better service.
e (10:00 p.m.)
One very interesting recommendation of the Glassco commission concerns the elimination of Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. If a department such as public works is in charge of the procurement and purchase of all material needed in structures occupied by the government, it is logical that the department should also be in a position to dispose of any surplus equipment owned by the government of Canada. We could save the Canadian taxpayer many thousands of dollars by eliminating Crown Assets Disposal Corporation.
The final recommendation of the Glassco royal commission was that the Department of Public Works be made responsible for the planning and supervision of all construction required by civil departments and agencies and the employment of all professional, technical and supporting staffs needed for such purposes; that it be responsible for the planning and supervision of construction for the Department of National Defence of all classes of property other than those at present provided for through the planning and construction staffs of the armed forces. We are very
June 29, 1967

anxious to go back into committee at a later date in order to inquire of the minister and his officers exactly how many of these recommendations have been implemented and how many are in the process of being implemented.
In the committee I gave notice that I was interested in hearing from the minister the policy the government has adopted concerning the construction of marinas, or the subsidies and grants that would be made available across this country to those interested in constructing marinas. As everyone knows, more and more people now have extra time on their hands. These people are interested in boating and they are travelling quite a long way in pleasure craft. They need protection as they travel along our coastlines and our larger lakes.
Not very many months ago the minister wrote me a letter stating in general the policy of the department in so far as help in the construction of marinas was concerned. At that time my immediate reaction was that there was a lack of regional approach to such a policy. Any policy concerning marinas applies right across the country. I am sure, Mr. Chairman, you will agree with me that if all policies of the government were applied across the country, without any regional consideration, we would not be rendering a service to the Canadian people.
In certain large metropolitan areas near the water marinas are built and operated at the expense of the boat owners. However, in other regions inhabited by people of limited means who work only 40 or 45 hours a week recreation is necessary, and if these people decide to go boating they need protection and the necessary structures to do so. Therefore I hope the letter which the minister wrote to me reflects a flexible policy which will not deprive many of our Canadians of the right to enjoy marina construction and marina privileges in their areas.
Another policy on which I should like the minister to comment concerns protective walls. This is a policy which no doubt has caused many headaches to the department, but at the same time it has caused large losses to many of our people who own land along the navigable waters. Ten or 15 years ago the government built protective walls in many of these areas, but since those days they have not been repaired or reconditioned. The result has been that the land owned by some of these people is being gradually eroded, and although the department may consider that a protective wall should only be built
Business of the House in an area where the cost would be justified in comparison with the value of the land to be protected, it seems to me we are forgetting that many of these people may not have the necessary income or the possibility of being able to move elsewhere.

So my question was, in part, to confirm or otherwise whether or not the Department of Fisheries, through the Fisheries Research Board, was responsible for this charter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I see that the Minister of Transport is playing a double header tonight. Though he said he had been raised to the exalted position of acting Minister of Fisheries, in the answer he gave just now, I hope that he will listen to me in his capacity as Minister of Transport, because it is in that capacity that I wish to direct to him a question, the answer to which I have been attempting to obtain on every day of this week, beginning with Monday.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
The headline on the editorial page of the Charlottetown Patriot last Saturday read: "Pickersgill Pickles Probe and Raises Ferry Fares." It is not hard to understand why the Minister of Transport should have issued his press release at a time when there was little opportunity to comment. I am not sure precisely when this press release was issued, but it seems it went out surreptitiously on Friday afternoon. In the course of this release he announced that a proposal which has been under consideration for some time will be followed through, and that there would be a substantial increase in ferry rates.
The minister himself did not think it was substantial. In answer to a question of mine yesterday he referred to it as being a very modest increase. Surely an increase of 33J per cent, from $3 to $4 for a visitor and auto, is not an inconsequential one to those who from time to time use this ferry system as the only means by which they can transport themselves and their vehicles between Prince Edward Island and the mainland.
The minister has on more than one occasion referred to this contemplated increase as a modest one. He is right, in one sense, because if we compare the amount which will be gained from this increase in revenue with the amount of the subsidy which is paid annually to provide the service I doubt whether in the coming year it will amount to as much as 2 per cent.
It is difficult to understand why the minister has taken this action, particularly when it follows only a few days after another action involving a further delay in the construction of the Northumberland strait crossing. If the

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion people of Prince Edward Island ever felt that a government in Ottawa fails to consider their needs and the many problems which face them, particularly with regard to transportation, surely in the past few weeks they have been strengthened in reaching such a conclusion. I think there is a question in the minds of many as to whether, when the government commits itself to one method of acting, it will follow through with its undertakings.
From time to time during the past year we have heard affirmations from the minister that a commission headed by Mr. Henry J. Darling would meet with all those affected by any possible increase in ferry rates. In May of last year, in answer to the junior member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie), he told us there would be a meeting of the commission to hear protests of this kind. Even as recently as April of this year, asked whether it was the intention of the government that hearings be held by the Canadian Maritime Commission into the rates charged on the ferry service, the answer was, yes.
In the light of these affirmative answers it is difficult to understand why the government would unilaterally, apparently without even notifying the provincial government, adopt a stance which at the very least shows a degree of insensitivity to the difficulties faced by Prince Edward Island in keeping a continuous link with the mainland.
Last year in the house I said there might be some sensible way in which a change could be made. The minister has provided, in this contemplated revision, that books of ten tickets would be made available to those using them within a two month period. It is true this would lower the cost to active shippers. But I am just as much concerned about those who travel less often, perhaps to visit family and friends in the same way as many of us drive from town to country and from country to town. If these books of ten tickets were valid for one year, the arrangement might have been agreeable and acceptable to those concerned.
Another possibility which might bring in just as much revenue as that which is now contemplated is an increase in fares on a temporary basis covering the active tourist season. When tourists have occasion to use the ferry only once or twice during the course of the year they probably would not mind paying an additional dollar or so, but to Prince Edward Islanders and maritimers generally this increased burden of 33J per

maintopic: TRANSPORT-INCREASE IN FERRY RATES, NEW BRUNSWICK-PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman made two points. One was that it had been the intention at one time to have an inquiry before any change was made. Two circumstances altered the view of the government, and my view as minister, about that. No representations were ever made to the government in any earlier period about there being any hardship through increasing the rates on ordinary motorcars for casual and occasional crossings. Considering the price of everything these days I do not think that a nine mile trip on a boat at $2 is very excessive. In fact I do not think the Prince Edward Islanders would like it to be represented that even they could not afford that for casual and occasional trips.
What we were concerned about, and properly concerned about, was the question of people who used these ferries commercially. We came to the conclusion that we had found a method that ought to be tried out before there would be much sense in having an inquiry into it, and that method, of course, involves no increase for anyone who makes ten trips in a two month period.
I also indicated in my statement the other day, and I do not think it is necessary to repeat it at this time and put it on the record again, that if there were cases of hardship, for instance of farmers delivering their own products where they would not be covered by this ten ticket arrangement, we would take a very sympathetic look at them; and we intend to do that. So far as the increase on casual, occasional crossings of an extra $1 on the round trip is concerned, I think it is still the cheapest trip on a boat anywhere in the world today, certainly anywhere in the western world.
A week has gone by and the hon. gentleman, as a good and assiduous representative of his riding, has done his best to keep this question alive. But the fact is that up to the last time I checked I had not received one word of protest from anyone in Prince Edward Island to suggest that my assessment of the situation, which is naturally the assessment of the government also, is far out. I think the hon. gentleman should be given full marks for trying.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman should devote himself to larger questions, and I would remind him that in the supplementary estimates


brought down yesterday there is another $21 million to be used to build all-weather roads in Prince Edward Island. I think that any little inconvenience from this ferry rate increase will be far more than offset by that good news of yesterday, added to the additional service that is to be provided for the summer months of this year.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question arises out of an article in the January-February-March Report on World Affairs, issued under the authority of the general council of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association. In that report I came on the following paragraph, referring to South-West Africa and South Africa:
Another move in the diplomatic offensive by South Africa to project a favourable picture of South-West Africa to the world was the invitation extended by the foreign minister, Dr. H. Muller, to ambassadors of all countries represented in South Africa to visit the booming territory and "see for themselves". Dr. Muller said that the government's attitude was that there was no aspect of South Africa's policy, either in the republic or in South-West Africa, that it need hide.
There was another paragraph which read:
Meanwhile in February the South African government had invited the diplomatic missions in Pretoria to visit South-West Africa to see for themselves what was being done for the indigenous inhabitants. By the end of March none of the diplomats had accepted the invitation, largely because they feared that such a visit might be construed as recognition of South Africa's right of jurisdiction over the territory.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
It might be suggested that the only possible visit to that area should be under the auspices of the United Nations. This, however, is not likely to happen because a mission from the United Nations went to South-West Africa in 1962. On invitation of the South African government the chairman and vice chairman of the special committee for South-West Africa, Mr. Victoria Carpio and Dr. Martinez de Alva, went to South-West Africa and, after a ten day visit issued a joint communique with the South African government in May 1962. This communique stated that they had found neither evidence of genocide in South-West Africa nor of militarization of the territory in violation of the terms of the mandate, and that there was no threat to international peace and security arising from South Africa's administration of the territory.
June 29, 1967	COMMONS
This report was immediately objected to by the United Nations and the two delegates were repudiated by that organization and by their own countries. So the United Nations carried on with the program, with which they seemed determined to proceed. The Canadian government in the most recent votes, admittedly, has abstained. They have not, however, opposed a policy which is totally unrealistic and one which involves a danger to world peace and security. South-West Africa has therefore been turned over to the mercies of the United Nations. Recent events have shown us the inadequacy of the United Nations to even maintain a peace keeping force in a troubled area. Where it will obtain the strength and power to undertake the task it is setting for itself is something I do not know.
I believe the Canadian government and the Department of External Affairs should be seriously concerned about the policy that is being set by the United Nations. The only question was whether the invitation had been received and, if so, whether it had been de-

It would either corroborate or deny the earlier report of the United Nations representatives who went to South-West Africa.
